paragraphs.heading: What the law says
paragraphs.text: Gauss's law is one of Maxwell's equations, the set that underpins classical electrodynamics. It connects the way electric charge is spread out with the electric field that charge produces. It also goes by the name Gauss's flux theorem.

paragraphs.heading: Flux through a closed surface
paragraphs.text: Picture any imaginary closed surface drawn around some charges; it is called a Gaussian surface. The electric flux is the electric field added up over that whole surface. The law says the net flux coming out equals the charge inside multiplied by 1/ε₀. It does not matter how that charge is arranged inside the surface.

paragraphs.heading: When symmetry helps
paragraphs.text: On its own, the total flux usually says little about the field, which can weave in and out of the surface in tangled patterns. But some problems have a symmetry that forces the field to cross the surface evenly. Then, once the total flux is known, the field can be worked out at every point. Spherical, cylindrical and planar symmetry are the usual cases.

paragraphs.heading: Two forms of one law
paragraphs.text: The version with flux over a surface is called the integral form. The differential form works point by point: it says the divergence of the field at a place is proportional to the charge per unit volume there. The two forms are mathematically the same, tied together by the divergence theorem. Each can also be written with the electric field E and all the charge, or with the displacement field D and the free charge only.

paragraphs.heading: Free and bound charge
paragraphs.text: Free charge is the kind met in simple cases, such as static electricity or the charge on a capacitor plate. Bound charge appears in materials that can be polarized: in an outside field, their electrons stay with their atoms but shift a tiny distance to one side. All those tiny shifts add up to a net spread of charge at large scale. There are often practical reasons to treat this bound charge separately, which is why the D form uses free charge alone.

paragraphs.heading: A cousin of Coulomb's law
paragraphs.text: Gauss's law and Coulomb's law can each be derived from the other. Neither follows from the other alone: getting Gauss's law from Coulomb's needs the superposition principle, the idea that the total field is the vector sum of the fields from each particle. Coulomb's law covers only charges at rest, yet Gauss's law holds for moving charges too. In that respect Gauss's law is the more general of the two.

paragraphs.heading: History and relatives
paragraphs.text: Joseph-Louis Lagrange first stated the law in 1773, and Carl Friedrich Gauss followed in 1835; both were studying how ellipsoids attract. Matching laws exist for magnetism and for gravity. In fact any inverse-square law can be written in the same shape, and Gauss's law for gravity is essentially Newton's law of gravity in another dress.
